title: The Long Portuguese Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino Portugués from Lisbon
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.
ai_disclosure: Written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), under the direction of CaminoPlus. Facts in the guides are listed with their sources; routes, closures and services change, so check local information before you walk.

spans.t: The long Portuguese Way starts at the cathedral of Lisbon and ends at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela. It follows the Tagus upstream across the flat farmland of the Ribatejo, reaches the Templar town of Tomar, passes the university city of Coimbra and reaches Porto after sixteen days. At Porto it joins the road that
The Portuguese Way

, another book in this series, describes day by day. The app's catalog gives the whole road ~620 km. This book walks it in 27 days and spends its pages on the part that book leaves out: the 16 days from Lisbon to Porto.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know whether this long road is your Camino, how its 27 walking days fall, region by region, and what to check before you leave home.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days, in three chapters from Lisbon to Porto, and the short chapter on the road beyond Porto. The chapter on other ways to split the days also gives the rule for the Compostela.
If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your day. Each one says what the walking is like, what is worth a pause, and where to take care.
If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way". Four weeks is a long time to imagine, and it is fine to decide later.
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change from season to season, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.

On this road they disagree more than most. No official page gives a stage list for the whole way, so the book follows published stage tables and says where they part company. Every distance carries a tilde,
, because it is approximate. Where something depends on the season (heat on the Tagus plain, a path after rain, a diversion), the book says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Caminho
is the Portuguese word for "way" or "road", and
Camino
the Spanish; this road has both names. Pilgrims greet each other with
bom caminho
in Portuguese and
Buen Camino
in Spanish. A
peregrino
is a pilgrim, in both languages. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card you carry and have stamped; a stamp is a
carimbo
in Portuguese and a
sello
in Spanish. The
Compostela
is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. The way is marked with yellow arrows, painted on walls, posts and paving stones.
They are explained again when they first matter, and used plainly after that.
Carry little, start early on the Tagus plain, and take your time over the hills after Tomar.
Bom caminho.
Where it starts and ends

The road starts at the Sé, the cathedral of Lisbon. Wikipedia says it was begun after the Christian conquest of the city in 1147, on the site of the main mosque, in a late Romanesque style. The yellow arrows begin there. From the Sé the way follows the Tagus upstream through Vila Franca de Xira and Azambuja to Santarém, Golegã and Tomar. The regional tourism board of Central Portugal takes over at Tomar and names Alvaiázere, Ansião and Coimbra, and after Coimbra Mealhada, Águeda, Albergaria-a-Velha, São João da Madeira and Grijó, before the road enters Porto.

The Xunta de Galicia, the regional government of Galicia, lists the places of the Portuguese Way in Portugal as Lisbon, Santarém, Coimbra, Porto, Barcelos, Ponte de Lima and Valença do Minho, where the Minho is crossed into Galicia. From Porto the road is the one
The Portuguese Way
describes: Barcelos, Ponte de Lima, Tui, Pontevedra, Padrón and the cathedral of Santiago.
How long
The CaminoPlus catalog gives the whole road as ~620 km. Sources differ:

items.t: The Confraternity of St James says ~640 km from Lisbon to Santiago via Porto, and ~252 km from Porto.
Wikipedia gives ~620 km in its box and ~610 km in its text.
One published stage table counts ~617 km in 27 stages. The sum of its 16 stages from Lisbon to Porto is ~374 km, and of its 11 from Porto ~242 km.
An older Confraternity sheet for the Lisbon to Porto stretch says ~380 km.

spans.t: This book follows that table's stage towns and numbers the days from 1 to 27. From Tomar to Porto they agree with the regional board's account, apart from Cernache, which the board calls a short detour. Other sources count 24 to 28 days for the whole road. None is the right one: stage towns depend on where people can sleep, and that changes. The days:

items.t: Day 2: Alpriate to Vila Franca de Xira, ~19 km
Day 3: Vila Franca de Xira to Azambuja, ~20 km
Day 14: Albergaria-a-Velha to São João da Madeira, ~29 km
Day 15: São João da Madeira to Grijó, ~19 km
Days 17 to 27: Porto to Santiago, eleven days, as

spans.t: What it feels like

Four landscapes follow one another. First the Tagus and its floodplain, the Ribatejo: flat, farmed, and long, with four stages in a row of ~30 km or more, much of it open to the sun. Then the limestone hills after Tomar, with olive groves, oak woods and Roman roads. Then the vineyards of the Bairrada and the small industrial towns of the district of Aveiro. Last, Porto, and the green north.

The CaminoPlus app's own note calls the road mostly flat, with some road sections. The Confraternity says the Lisbon to Porto stretch has plenty of road walking at first, becomes more beautiful after Santarém, and that the days between Tomar and Coimbra are delightful. It adds that the road is now well waymarked, but has less support for pilgrims than the road from Porto on.
Why it exists

The Xunta says the Portuguese road grew in importance from the twelfth century, after Portugal became independent, and that the country's north to south road network was organised around the pilgrimage, through Lisbon, Santarém, Coimbra and Porto. It names two Portuguese pilgrims: Elizabeth of Portugal, the "Holy Queen", who made the pilgrimage in the fourteenth century and was buried at Coimbra with a pilgrim's staff, and King Manuel I, who made the pilgrimage from Lisbon to Santiago in 1502. The regional board adds that Queen Teresa is said to have founded a hostel for pilgrims at Albergaria-a-Velha in 1117.

Wikipedia describes an older, western road from Lisbon, by the thermal hospital of Caldas da Rainha and the monastery of Alcobaça, and says that pilgrims used Roman roads to reach Coimbra and had to reach Porto before the city gates closed at night. The road you walk today is the one the stage tables and the regional board describe: the Tagus road.
Company on the road

Wikipedia, reporting the Pilgrim's Office statistics, says that in 2025 the Portuguese Way was the second most walked route to Santiago, with 19 per cent of pilgrims, and that most who received the Compostela started in Tui (41 per cent), Porto (26 per cent) or Valença (18 per cent). Together those three starts make 85 per cent, so every other start, Lisbon included, shares the remaining 15 per cent. The Confraternity says that most pilgrims start in Porto but many walk from Lisbon.
Read together, these suggest a quiet road before Porto. That is a reading of the numbers, not a promise.
How hard is it?

The app's catalog rates this road 3 on a scale of 1 to 5. It rates the Camino Francés 3 as well, the Portuguese Way from Porto 2 and the Camino del Norte 4. The rating is a rough guide, and the catalog does not say what it weighs. Here the honest reading is that nothing on the road is steep for long, and almost everything about it is long.

The length is the first difficulty: about four weeks, not two. The second is the run of long days at the start. One published table has four stages in a row of ~30 km or more, from Azambuja to Alvaiázere, with stretches open to the sun. The third is the surface. The Confraternity's older sheet for the stretch to Porto (written for it in 2013, and dated) puts the walking at at least three quarters on asphalt, on industrial estates, quiet rural roads and residential streets, and notes reports of heavy lorry traffic on national roads. That was the author's estimate, and routes change, so treat it as a warning, not a measurement. Expect hard ground, and look after your feet.

The hills are modest. That table marks the first serious climbs after Tomar, in the limestone hills of the Serra de Sicó, and calls the stage into Santarém demanding because of its final climb. It rates two of its 16 stages Hard, Azambuja to Santarém and Tomar to Alvaiázere, both ~32 km or more.
Who it suits

It suits a walker who has four weeks and wants a road with a shape: a capital, a river, a Templar town, a university city, Porto, and then the border and the arrival. It suits people who like their history in stone and in old roads. The regional board's guide follows stretches of Roman road, and Wikipedia says Conímbriga was a junction on the Roman road that linked Lisbon and Braga.

It suits people who can be alone. The road before Porto may have few other pilgrims, if the statistics are a guide, and it has less pilgrim infrastructure than the road from Porto on, as the Confraternity says. If you like a quiet road and are comfortable planning a night ahead, that may be what you want.
Who might choose another
If you want the company of the albergues and a dense network of hostels, start in Porto.
The Portuguese Way
describes that road, and the Confraternity says the road from Porto is better supported.
If you have two or three weeks, not four, start at Coimbra, which is 17 stages from Santiago on the table this book follows, or at Porto, which is 11. The chapter on before you go gives the lengths.
If you want the sea, the Coastal Way leaves the Central route soon after Porto, and has its own book in this series,
The Coastal Way
. If you want mountains, the French Way, ~773 km in the catalog, crosses the Pyrenees and the mountains of León.

If you cannot walk ~30 km on a hard surface and then do it again two days later, start later. On this book's days the longest from Coimbra is ~29 km, and the older sheet warns that on the way to Porto some days of ~30 km or more are unavoidable, because buses are very infrequent.
Questions worth asking yourself

items.t: Can you walk ~20 km on a hard surface, two or three days in a row, with your pack, and add a few kilometres?
Do you want the whole road from Lisbon, or the best of it, from Santarém, Tomar or Coimbra?
How do you feel about walking alone for days, through suburbs and farmland, before the road fills up at Porto?
What do you want from the walk: sport, solitude, history, a rest, prayer, a promise kept? Every answer is a good one, and the road does not ask.

spans.t: If most of your answers are yes, and the others are "we shall see", you are ready for the next chapter.

This road starts on a dry, hot plain and ends in a green, wet corner of Spain. The regional tourism board of Central Portugal, in its guide to the Caminhos de Santiago, says that spring and autumn are the best seasons, because summer and winter can be very harsh. The Confraternity of St James describes northern Portugal and Galicia as a changeable maritime climate, with westerly winds and generous rain, and calls early autumn fairly dry and settled. Everything below is a pattern, not a forecast.
Three climates in one walk
The Tagus valley (Days 1 to 6).

This is the hot part. Wikipedia's tables (1991 to 2020) give a mean daytime high in Lisbon of ~28 °C in July and ~29 °C in August, and in Santarém of ~31 °C in July and ~32 °C in August. Rain is nearly absent: ~3 mm in July in Lisbon and ~5 mm in August. Lisbon's record is ~44 °C, set in August 2018, Wikipedia says. The days here are long, and part of the way runs along an open flood levee with little shade.
Tomar to Porto (Days 7 to 16).
Milder. Coimbra's mean high is ~28 °C in July, and its record, in the same tables, ~41.6 °C. Rain grows as you go north: a year brings ~608 mm in Santarém and ~866 mm in Coimbra.
Porto and Galicia (Days 17 to 27).

Cooler and much wetter. At Porto airport the mean high in July is ~24 °C and the year brings ~1,147 mm of rain. At Santiago the July high is ~25 °C and the year brings ~1,527 mm, with ~214 mm in October.
The seasons
Spring.

A rewarding time, the Confraternity says, cool, with fresh growth in the north. In the south the plain is not yet at its hottest: Lisbon's mean high in May is ~23 °C. Rain is still common further north: ~96 mm in April at Porto airport.
Summer.

The board calls it harsh, and the numbers show why on the plain. The board advises making the way by day, preferably in the morning, and avoiding the hottest hours. A heatwave on a ~33 km day, such as Day 4, is a safety matter, not a discomfort. In the north, the Confraternity adds, summer can be hot and humid and the peak holiday months crowded. Wikipedia says most pilgrims on the Portuguese Way finish between May and September.
Autumn.

September is still warm in Lisbon, with a mean high of ~27 °C, and rain returns slowly: ~39 mm in September, ~111 mm in October and ~134 mm in November. At Porto airport October brings ~149 mm and at Santiago ~214 mm.
Winter.

Mild and damp, and short. The mean high in January is ~15 °C in Lisbon and ~12 °C at Santiago. Rain in January is ~104 mm in Lisbon and ~196 mm at Santiago. Wikipedia says frost at Santiago is common only from December to February, about 13 days a year, and snow rare, two or three days. The trouble in winter is rain and the light, not cold.
Daylight

Computed for each city (a standard solar calculation), Lisbon has about nine and a half hours of daylight at the winter solstice and about fifteen at the summer solstice. Santiago has about nine and about fifteen. In December the sun rises at about eight in the morning in Lisbon and about nine in Santiago, and sets at about twenty past five and about six. In June it sets at about five past nine in Lisbon and about a quarter past ten in Santiago, by the local clocks.

The clocks change at the border. Wikipedia says continental Portugal keeps Western European Time, and peninsular Spain, Galicia included, Central European Time, an hour ahead. Your phone will jump, and your breakfast plan should jump with it.
A month, in a line each

items.t: cool, and wet in the north. Lisbon's mean high is ~19 °C in March.
mild on the plain, with highs of ~23 and ~26 °C in Lisbon, and the days at their longest.
hot and dry on the plain, and the hardest time for the first six days.
warm, and the rain starts to come back.
wet, with the days shortening. The National Horse Fair takes place in Golegã in November, Wikipedia says, so ask about beds if you pass then.

spans.t: Check before you go

Before any date, look for diversions, closures and, in hot dry weather, heat and fire warnings from the national weather services. The Tagus levee and some farm tracks can be overgrown or boggy at the wrong time of year, as the older Confraternity sheet says. Tomar's Festa dos Tabuleiros is held every four years, most recently in June and July 2023 according to Wikipedia, so the next may fall in 2027: if you plan to pass Tomar in early summer, ask.
The credencial
The
credencial

is your pilgrim's passport, and you need one before the first stamp. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago says the official model is a cardboard card of sixteen concertina-folded pages, with boxes for the stamps, and that it has two practical purposes: access to the hostels of the Way, and proof when you ask for the Compostela. It also describes a digital credential, a phone app. Carry the paper card in any case.

In Portugal, Via Lusitana, the pilgrims' association that works on the waymarking and upkeep of the Portuguese ways, says on its site that two official models of the credencial are available: the cathedral's own and one that the association issues with the cathedral's authorisation. You can ask the association for it through its website. The regional tourism board's guide of 2023 adds that credenciais were also to be had at the Sé of Lisbon and at the two cathedrals of Coimbra. Ask before you rely on that.
Stamps,
carimbos

in Portuguese, are normally collected where you sleep, and also in parish churches, monasteries, town halls and other places, the Office says; Via Lusitana adds tourist offices. The older Confraternity sheet adds that south of Porto, where the road was little known in 2013, you may have to be inventive: post offices, parish council offices, town halls and railway stations gave stamps.
Getting there

Lisbon airport lies ~7 km north-east of the historic centre, Wikipedia says, and has its own metro station. The Confraternity notes that you can also fly into Porto, Vigo or Santiago, and that a regular bus runs between Santiago and Porto in about four hours, so flying home from either end of the road is possible. Timetables change: check the current ones when you plan your return.
Choosing your start
Where you begin sets the length of your walk. On the table this book follows, the road from each start to Santiago is:

The Confraternity says the way becomes more beautiful after Santarém, and that the days between Tomar and Coimbra are delightful. That is a reason to start at Santarém or Tomar if you cannot spare four weeks. The app's own note suggests adding about two weeks to a start in Porto. For the whole road, 27 walking days and a rest day each at Tomar, Coimbra and Porto make about 30 days, and you need a day each to travel there and back. If you are choosing a start with the Compostela in mind, read the rule in the chapter on other ways to split the days first, and ask the Pilgrim's Office.
Training

The regional board advises starting five months before, and building up the distance on varied ground with some hills. For this road add one thing: the length of your longest day. Four stages in a row of ~30 km or more ask a lot of a body that has not walked far in months, and the surface is hard. A few weeks of regular walking will do more than any programme, so train in the shoes and with the pack you will carry.
Shoes and feet

Much of the road is asphalt, and tracks beside the Tagus. Look for a cushioned sole and a little room in the toe box, because feet swell as the day goes on. Break your shoes in before you leave. Two pairs of socks, changed at lunch, are a cheap defence against blisters. Treat a hot spot when you feel it, not when it has become a blister. If something hurts in a way that grows and does not fade, rest it, and see a doctor.
Packing

Pack light, and then lighter: the board advises a pack of no more than ten kilograms. The essentials are plain: sun protection, a hat and a water bottle, because the first week has little shade; a rain jacket, because the road ends in the green north; a small first-aid kit for feet; a head torch and earplugs for shared rooms; and, as the board's list says, a sleeping bag and slippers. A phone with an offline map is a good tool and a poor single plan. Know your next town before the battery is low. Leave whatever you are unsure of at home.
Money, language and the clock
Portugal and Spain both use the euro. Carry some coins and small notes for small purchases. Prices are not in this book; the people you meet will tell you what things cost.
Portuguese is spoken until the border. In Galicia there are two official languages, Galician and Spanish. Pilgrims need little:
bom dia
("good morning"),
obrigado
(a man says thank you) or
obrigada
(a woman does), and in Galicia
grazas
or
gracias
. Say them with a smile and you will be understood. Remember the clock: Galicia is an hour ahead of Portugal.
Emergencies
The European emergency number is 112, in Portugal as in Spain. Keep it in your head, not just in your phone.

chapters.title: Lisbon and the Tagus: Days 1 to 6

spans.t: The character of these days

Six days from the cathedral of Lisbon to Tomar, ~156 km on the figures of one published table. The first two days leave a capital and its suburbs. The next four follow the Tagus upstream across the Ribatejo, the flat, farmed floodplain, and the last three of them are ~30 km or more. Wikipedia calls the Tagus the longest river in the Iberian Peninsula.

A note on the figures. The regional tourism board of Central Portugal begins its account at Tomar. Visit Portugal's page on the road could not be read, because it asks every visitor to pass a bot check. And the CaminoPlus catalog holds no stage data for this route. So these days rest on two published stage tables and on the Confraternity of St James, whose practical sheet for the stretch to Porto, called here the older sheet, dates from 2013. Where they disagree, this book says so. All three stage lists agree on the towns from Azambuja to Tomar. They disagree about where the first days end.
Day 1: Lisbon to Alpriate (~22 km)

You start at the Sé. The arrows begin there, and in the old streets many are painted low on the wall. The way crosses the old quarters, runs beside the Tagus and passes through the Parque das Nações, the district laid out in 1998 for the World Exposition, according to Wikipedia. It leaves the city at Sacavém and ends at Alpriate, a farming hamlet, in ~22 km by the table.

Plans for this day differ. Another table ends it at Santa Iría de Azoia, ~19 km. The older Confraternity sheet offers several choices, from a ~8 km walk to the Parque das Nações to ~37 km in a day. Beyond Sacavém it calls the way an unlovely walk through industrial estates beside an old canal, but very well marked.
Day 2: Alpriate to Vila Franca de Xira (~19 km)

A short, flat day, with the river close. The way passes Póvoa de Santa Iria and Alverca, and in places follows boardwalks beside the Tagus. The table warns about a stretch of road before Alhandra. From there a path along the river, paved, leads to Vila Franca de Xira.

Wikipedia says the municipality lies on both banks of the Tagus, ~32 km north-east of Lisbon, and is best known for its bull-running festivals, in July and October. The older sheet says the arrows pass the bullring. Another table gives this day as ~22 km, from a different start.
Day 3: Vila Franca de Xira to Azambuja (~20 km)

All three stage lists agree: ~20 km. The table describes it as a transition day through the farming heart of the Ribatejo, on the floodplain beside the railway. The older sheet calls the way industrial parks, then a national road with a wide shoulder into Azambuja: unpleasant, it says, but not dangerous. Where there is no path, walk on the shoulder, facing the traffic.
Wikipedia places Azambuja in the district of Lisbon but in the old province of the Ribatejo. Sleep early: tomorrow is the first hard day.
Day 4: Azambuja to Santarém (~33 km)

The first hard day. Tables give ~32 or ~33 km. The table calls it one of the longest and most demanding days of the whole road, and very exposed to the sun. You follow the Tagus, sometimes along the top of the flood levee, to Valada and Porto de Muge. Then comes a lonely stretch of farmland with no shade and no services, and the last climb up into Santarém. The older sheet agrees, noting about nine kilometres of farm track with no facilities and a levee path that can be overgrown, with a road below it.

Start at first light. Carry lunch and more water than you think you need. Santarém stands on a plateau above the river, ~65 km north-east of Lisbon, and Wikipedia calls it the "Capital of the Portuguese Gothic". Its church of Graça holds the Gothic tomb of Pedro de Meneses, and Pedro Álvares Cabral lies under a plain slab near the main chapel. The Confraternity says the road becomes more beautiful after Santarém.
Day 5: Santarém to Golegã (~31 km)

You leave through the São Tiago gate in the old walls, the Gate of Santiago, and go down the hill. Tables give ~30.5 to ~30.7 km. The way is easy and flat, on farm tracks among vineyards and fields, by Vale de Figueira and Pombalinho, and through Azinhaga, where José Saramago was born in 1922, Wikipedia says. He won the Nobel Prize in 1998.

Watch the arrows. The older sheet reports that in 2013 the waymarking and the route around Azinhaga were disputed locally, with two ways in use. Follow the arrows you find, and ask. Golegã, the horse capital of Portugal, has an early sixteenth-century church with a Manueline portal, and holds its National Horse Fair every November.
Day 6: Golegã to Tomar (~31 km)

The tables split here, and by a lot: two give ~31 km, the older sheet ~22 km. It is the largest disagreement on the Tagus road, and this book cannot settle it. Ask at Golegã, and plan for the longer figure.

The way leaves the Tagus after São Caetano and passes Vila Nova da Barquinha and Atalaia, whose parish church is a national monument. Near Vila Nova da Barquinha the regional board's account of the Central Way begins, and it says the road through its region was officially certified in July 2023. Tomar follows. The Templars built their castle and convent there in the twelfth century, and the Convent of Christ has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983, with the round Charola of the twelfth century. The long Pegões aqueduct, ~6 km, was built between 1503 and 1614. If you want a day off the road, Tomar is a good place.
The character of these days

Four days, ~92 km on the table's figures, from the Templar town to the university city. The plain ends at Tomar. The way climbs into the limestone hills of the Serra de Sicó, among olive groves, vines and oak woods, and follows old Roman roads. The Confraternity calls the stages between Tomar and Coimbra delightful.

This is where the regional board's account takes over. It lists Tomar, Alvaiázere, Rabaçal and Coimbra as its stage places, and its article on the road names Ansião as well. The table this book follows adds Ansião and Cernache, which shortens the days. Others join Alvaiázere to Rabaçal in one long day: the older Confraternity sheet gives ~33 km. Choose by your legs, and ask where you can sleep.
Day 7: Tomar to Alvaiázere (~32 km)

The first serious climbs. You leave through the old centre, cross the Nabão by the bridge of King Manuel I and go out by the old road towards Coimbra. The regional board says the way follows a stretch of the Roman road that once linked Tomar with Conímbriga. Then come ups and downs through olive groves, vines and native woodland, with outcrops of limestone from the Sicó massif.

Tables give ~31 to ~32 km, so this is a long day on tired legs, after three days of ~30 km. Wikipedia places Alvaiázere in the district of Leiria. Its name comes from an Arabic word that means "the falconer". Ask the night before where you can buy lunch.
Day 8: Alvaiázere to Ansião (~23 km)

A shorter, easier day, a rest for the legs after the last one. The way crosses the Serra de Ariques, among holm oaks and olive trees. The older sheet makes Alvaiázere to Rabaçal one day of ~33 km, so this is the day on which you decide which plan you are walking.
The regional board's guide tells a local legend about Ansião: that its name comes from alms given by Queen Isabel, the Holy Queen, to a poor old man,
um ancião
. A bridge at the edge of town is tied to her pilgrimage. It is a legend, and a pleasant one for a day that asks little.
Day 9: Ansião to Cernache (~26 km)

The table calls this one of the loveliest days since Lisbon, and an easy one. It is mostly a gentle descent by old Roman roads and paths among vines, olive groves and woods along streams. At Rabaçal there is a Roman villa, whose mosaics the regional board dates to the fourth and fifth centuries, and a local cheese with a protected name.

The highlight comes at the end: Conímbriga. Wikipedia says it was not the largest Roman city in Portugal but is the best preserved, a national monument since 1910, ~16 km from Coimbra. It lay on the Roman road that linked Lisbon and Braga. Its museum opened in 1962, and the House of Fountains has mosaics of hunting scenes. The older sheet suggests splitting the day at the ruins: ~11 km from Rabaçal and ~21 km on to Coimbra. The regional board's guide describes Cernache as a short detour from the waymarked line, and the tables name it as a night stop, so ask.
Day 10: Cernache to Coimbra (~11 km)
The shortest day of the road. Table distances differ by a few kilometres, because another table starts the day at Condeixa-a-Nova, ~16 km out. Either way you reach Coimbra early. Keep the afternoon.

The way climbs gently, past the remains of an old aqueduct, to the quarters above the city, and crosses the Mondego. Coimbra was the capital of Portugal from 1131 to 1255, Wikipedia says. Its university, which Wikipedia says dates from 1290 and has been in Coimbra for good since 1537, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 2013, and has an eighteenth-century Baroque library, the Joanina. On the south bank of the river is the monastery of Santa Clara-a-Nova, where Queen Isabel's Gothic tomb stands. The regional board says it shows the shell, the cross of Santiago and the pilgrim's staff, and the Xunta says she was buried with her staff.

The Old Cathedral, the Sé Velha, was begun in the twelfth century, and the church of Santa Cruz is the national pantheon, with the tombs of the first two kings of Portugal. Coimbra is a good place for a rest day, and the easiest on this road to defend.
The character of these days

Six days, ~127 km on the table's figures, through the Bairrada and the district of Aveiro. It is a landscape of small towns that run into one another, vineyards, pine and eucalyptus woods, and industrial estates, with the suburbs of Porto at the end. The days are moderate: the table rates two of the six Moderate, four Easy, and none Hard. The regional board's account follows the road as far as Albergaria-a-Velha, and its guide says the way runs along Roman roads here, with strong medieval marks.
Take care with the figures. Tables differ here by ~3 to ~7 km a day, most on Day 12.
Day 11: Coimbra to Mealhada (~25 km)

You cross the Mondego and walk on tracks and minor roads, over rolling ground, through pine and eucalyptus woods and the first vineyards of the Bairrada. The villages follow one another so closely that the table advises keeping an eye on the arrows. Tables give ~23, ~25 and ~26 km.
Wikipedia says the Bairrada is well known for its vineyards and its wine industry. The regional board mentions the sparkling wines and the roast suckling pig,
leitão
, of the Bairrada, and a Roman milestone, ~1.8 m high, in the entrance to the town hall of Mealhada, part of the Roman road that linked Lisbon and Braga.
Day 12: Mealhada to Águeda (~24 km)

A transition day, the table says, with a gentle profile and plenty of settlements: villages, farmland and the odd industrial estate, with stretches of asphalt that deserve extra care. The sources disagree here more than on any other day: ~24, ~25 and ~31 km. The older Confraternity sheet has the longest, and does not say why. Ask locally, and do not plan the night on a single figure.

The regional board says the arrows point towards Avelãs de Caminho, in the municipality of Anadia, and then on to Águeda. It describes Águeda as known today for the urban art of its centre. The municipality also holds the Pateira de Fermentelos, which the board calls the largest natural lagoon in the Iberian Peninsula.
Day 13: Águeda to Albergaria-a-Velha (~16 km)

A short day, the table says, good for resting your legs, and one of the most beautiful of this part. The way climbs gradually out of the Águeda valley and, from Pedaçães, follows dirt paths through thick vegetation. Tables give ~16 to ~19.5 km.
The regional board says you cross the old bridge over the Marnel, a tributary of the Vouga, at Lamas do Vouga before reaching Albergaria-a-Velha. The town's name comes from
albergaria

, an old word for a hostel, and the board's guide says it goes back to the one that Queen Teresa is said to have founded for pilgrims in 1117. Wikipedia records a donation of the lands of Albergaria in the same year.
Day 14: Albergaria-a-Velha to São João da Madeira (~29 km)

The longest day of the week, and the tables agree: ~29 km. It runs on dirt tracks through pine and eucalyptus woods and small settlements, in a landscape that grows steadily more built up. You cross the old centres of Bemposta and Oliveira de Azeméis. Wikipedia calls Oliveira an industrial centre, ~35 km south of Porto. Two short days remain to Porto.
Start early, and ask in Albergaria in the morning where you can buy lunch.
Day 15: São João da Madeira to Grijó (~19 km)

An urban day that tells you Porto is near: mostly asphalt, with an occasional short, steep climb. The way crosses the old centre of Arrifana and climbs towards Escapães. Another table gives ~16 km, so ask at São João. Grijó is the last town the regional board names before Porto.
Day 16: Grijó to Porto (~15 km)

A short day through Vila Nova de Gaia, between streets and the odd park, with the best ending of the road: you cross the Douro on the Dom Luís I Bridge into Porto. Wikipedia says its upper deck was inaugurated in 1886, that it carries pedestrians and the metro, and that the lower deck carries road traffic, cyclists and walkers. The older sheet describes a high crossing, which leads to the upper town near the cathedral, and a low one, by the riverside. Decide which you want before the arrow sends you down.
You arrive at the Sé, the cathedral of Porto, where
The Portuguese Way
begins its first day. Here the road you have walked joins the road described in that book. Mark the moment: you have walked about 374 km, and ~242 km remain.

chapters.title: From Porto to Santiago: Days 17 to 27

spans.t: Where the roads join
At the Sé of Porto the Lisbon road becomes the Central route of the Camino Portugués, the road that
The Portuguese Way

describes day by day. No page this book could read says exactly where the two meet. The Confraternity's older sheet for the Lisbon to Porto stretch ends at the cathedral, and the published tables for the road from Porto begin there. So this book takes the Sé as the meeting point, and does not repeat the eleven days that follow.

They are Days 17 to 27 of this book: Porto to Vilarinho, then Barcelos, Ponte de Lima, Rubiães and Tui, where you cross the Minho into Spain; then O Porriño, Redondela, Pontevedra, Caldas de Reis, Padrón and Santiago. The catalog gives Porto to Santiago ~240 km, the table this book follows ~242 km, and the Confraternity ~252 km. Day 17 is Day 1 of that book, and its chapters on the days take over from here.
What changes at Porto

items.t: Wikipedia reports that in 2025 most pilgrims who received the Compostela had started at Tui, Porto or Valença, all on this stretch.

The Confraternity says yellow arrows are plentiful from the cathedral at Porto to the border, thanks to the Associação dos Amigos do Caminho Português de Santiago, and that in Galicia granite pillars add the distance to Santiago. It also says the road from Porto has more pilgrim infrastructure than the road before it.
The Minho is the border, and Galicia is an hour ahead of Portugal. Portuguese gives way to Galician and Spanish.

spans.t: Choices at Porto

A walker from Lisbon can also take the Coastal Way. The Confraternity says it leaves the Central route soon after Porto, follows the shore, and meets the Central route again at Redondela. It has its own book in this series,
The Coastal Way

. The Confraternity also describes a Litoral route that leaves Porto along the Douro and the sea, and the Spiritual Variant, which leaves the Central route at Pontevedra and goes by boat from Vilanova de Arousa up the estuary to Pontecesures. Each has its own waymarks, so know which road you are on, and ask locally about the boat before you plan around it.

chapters.title: Other ways to split the days, other roads, and the Compostela rule

spans.t: Other ways to split the days

The 27 days in this book are one plan among several. Sources count 24 to 28 days for the whole road, and the older Confraternity sheet plans only 13 days from Lisbon to Porto, against this book's 16. Here are the commonest changes.

items.t: The first days end in different places in different plans. This book stops at Alpriate and Vila Franca de Xira. Another table stops at Santa Iría de Azoia and Vila Franca (~19 and ~22 km). The older sheet joins them in one day of ~37 km, and also offers a ~8 km first day to the Parque das Nações or a ~11 km one to Sacavém, for those who want a gentle start and can return to Lisbon.
Golegã to Tomar is ~31 km in two tables and ~22 km in the older sheet. Ask locally before you choose.

From Alvaiázere to Coimbra, this book takes three days: ~23, ~26 and ~11 km. The regional board names Rabaçal as the stage place, and the older sheet joins Alvaiázere to Rabaçal (~33 km) and Rabaçal to Coimbra (~32 km), or splits the second at Conímbriga (~11 and ~21 km). Another table goes by Condeixa-a-Nova.

The older sheet plans Coimbra to Porto in five days of ~26, ~31, ~19.5, ~29 and ~35 km. This book makes it six, by stopping at Grijó, which is also where the regional board's article puts the last stop before Porto.
Tomar, Coimbra and Porto are the natural places, and Tomar comes after the three longest days.

spans.t: Whatever you choose, the arithmetic is the same: ~620 km on the catalog's figure, ~23 km a day over 27 days, less on the short days and more on the long.
Other roads
Fátima.

The Confraternity says you can detour to Fátima from Santarém. The older sheet adds that in the first days from Lisbon the arrows are shared with markers for the Fátima way. Blue arrows and the Fátima markers belong to that road, so follow the yellow ones to Santiago.
The western road.

Wikipedia describes an older way from Lisbon by Caldas da Rainha and Alcobaça. The regional board's guide of 2023 lists a Caminho do Oeste as "in development", based on written accounts of the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, by places such as Torres Vedras, Óbidos, Alcobaça and Batalha, and a Caminho Marítimo by the ports of the coast, also in development. For the ways not yet waymarked, the board says, you must bring the information and the GPS tracks you need. Neither is the road of this book.
The Coastal Way and the Spiritual Variant
leave the road after Porto and Pontevedra. The chapter on the road beyond Porto says where.
The Compostela rule

The Compostela is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for religious and/or spiritual reasons and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback. The Office asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route. On foot or on horseback, the Office asks for at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that it recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the Cathedral.

The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.

The Way may be done in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and the end of each stage, with the date. A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain. The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.
From Lisbon the road is ~620 km, far more than the last hundred kilometres the Office asks for. The Office decides, and rules change: ask it in any doubt.
Albergue life, and its absence
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: a dormitory with bunk beds, a shared bathroom and often a place to wash your clothes. You show your credencial at the door, and the host, the
hospitalero

, stamps it and tells you the house rules. The Pilgrim's Office says hostels without subsidies are kept going by what pilgrims contribute. Leave a place cleaner than you found it, and give what you can.

Between Lisbon and Porto the network is thinner than on the road from Porto. The Confraternity says the road has less support for pilgrims, but that new albergues open every year and it is much easier now than it was five years before. Via Lusitana publishes a list of hostels on its site, and warns that the information may sometimes be out of date. Some places on it ask for a donation,
donativo

, and not a fixed sum. The sources also mention guesthouses, rural houses, parish houses and youth hostels, and the older sheet records that in 2013 some volunteer fire stations gave pilgrims a room for a donation, a courtesy that was becoming rarer. Via Lusitana suggests that when you stay in a hotel or guesthouse you say you are a pilgrim and show your credencial, since some give a discount.

Which places exist, which are open this month, and whether you can book differ from town to town and change from season to season. This book does not list them. Use the CaminoPlus app for where to sleep tonight, ask locally for tomorrow, and do not rely on one source before a long day such as Day 4.
The etiquette of a dormitory is short and kind.

items.t: Arrive, claim a bed, shower, wash and hang out your clothes. The evening is for resting.
Keep your voice low after the lights go out, and do not rustle bags at night or before dawn. Pack your rucksack in the hall.
Use a head torch, not the main light. Silence your phone.
Keep your pack and shoes off the bed.
Earplugs are a small comfort that goes a long way. Somebody will snore, and if it is you, apologise at breakfast.

spans.t: Bedbugs

are a risk in any shared bed. Check the seams of the mattress, keep your pack off the bed, and if you find bites, tell the host and wash and dry everything hot. It is not a reason to avoid hostels, only a reason to look before you lie down.
If you are ill, tired or sleeping badly, take a private room. It is not cheating. A good night is part of the walk.
Eating
The regional board's guide points to what each stretch is known for. At Tomar it recommends the convent sweets, the
doçaria conventual

. At Coimbra it names the Santa Clara pastries, a convent sweet too. At Mealhada, the sparkling wines and the roast suckling pig of the Bairrada. In Águeda, the local pastry. At Rabaçal, a local cheese with a protected name.
You do not need to eat all of it. Pick one local thing a day, and eat it without a screen.

Water matters more than food. Fill your bottle in each town. On Day 4 the table speaks of a long stretch with no shade and no services, and the older sheet counts about nine kilometres without any facilities near the end, so carry lunch and water from Azambuja. On other days ask the evening before where you can buy your lunch.
Resting
It is easy to treat the walk as a timetable to be kept. Resist that. A day of rest is part of the walk.

On this road the three natural places for it are Tomar, after the three longest days; Coimbra, a city that rewards more than a morning; and Porto, at the end of the Lisbon road and the start of the Porto one. The other place is the end. Santiago is a city built for the end of a pilgrimage, and it deserves more than a night.

On the road, listen to your body before you listen to your plan. Take the short days as short days. If something hurts in a way that grows rather than fades, stop, rest, and let a doctor look at it. You are not walking to prove anything.
Feet

On a road that is mostly asphalt, your feet take the weight. Look after them at lunch, not in the evening: shoes off, socks changed, a hot spot treated before it becomes a blister. Hard surfaces tire shins and knees as well as soles, so shorten a day before you push through a pain that is growing.
Heat

This is the main danger of the first week, and it can build quickly. The Tagus plain is hot and dry in summer, and part of Day 4 is open farmland with no shade and no services. The regional tourism board's advice is plain: make the way by day, preferably in the morning, avoid the hottest hours, and shelter from shortly before sunset until daybreak. It also advises drinking regularly and stopping for ten minutes every two hours, to rest and eat a little.

items.t: Start at first light in summer, and plan to finish before the afternoon.
Carry more water than you think you need on the long days, and fill up at every town.
Wear a hat and sun protection. Carry something to eat.
If you feel faint, sick or confused, stop in the shade, drink, and ask for help. Call 112 if it does not pass.
If the forecast is for a heatwave, do not walk a ~33 km day. Shorten it, or rest.

spans.t: Roads, tracks and railways

Much of the way runs beside national roads and through industrial estates. The Confraternity advises, when you must walk on a road, to stay aware of the traffic and use the strip between the road and the drainage ditch. Where there is no path, walk on the shoulder, facing the traffic, and cross where you can see and be seen. The older sheet says the shoulders on the national roads are usually wide, and also reports heavy lorry traffic at some times, so stay alert at junctions and roundabouts.
A published stage description mentions railway lines that the way runs beside or crosses, some of the crossings without barriers. Stop, look both ways, and listen.
On the flood levee of the Tagus the path can be overgrown at some times of the year, and the older sheet says a road runs below it. Use the road when the levee is overgrown or wet.
Rain and wet

The north is wet, as the chapter on when to go says. A proper rain jacket and a plan for wet feet matter more in the last third of the road than in the first. Wet stone paving, in old towns and on old roads, is slippery. Go slowly on descents.
Fire and closures

In hot, dry weather, wildfire can close paths and roads. Follow any closure, diversion or instruction of the local authorities, and do not argue with a sign. Before you set out each morning, ask your host about the day's route, and about any diversion.
When to stop

Stopping is a skill. You are not walking to prove anything. If something hurts in a way that grows and does not fade, rest it for a day, and let a doctor look at it. If you are alone on a quiet stretch, tell someone where you plan to sleep. The European emergency number is 112, in Portugal as in Spain.

People walk to Santiago for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work, a promise made long ago. A road of four weeks has room for all of them, and it gives something that shorter roads give less of: time. Time to be bored, to be tired, to stop being either, and to find out what is left.
A long road starts slowly

The first days are the least photogenic. You leave a capital on foot, through old quarters, then suburbs, a canal, industrial estates and the shoulder of a national road. There is nothing to be done about that except to walk it slowly. These places belong to the pilgrimage as much as the Roman road after Tomar, and the walker who learns to be present in them has learned something that the pretty days will not teach.

Then the plain opens, and the long days begin. A day of ~30 km on flat ground is a different thing from a climb. It has no summit and no reward at the top. It has a rhythm, a horizon that does not change, and your own thoughts, for hours. Some people find that hard and some find it a gift. You will know by the third day.
Those who came before

Others have walked this road with their reasons. The Xunta de Galicia names two Portuguese pilgrims: Elizabeth of Portugal, the Holy Queen, who made the pilgrimage in the fourteenth century and was buried at Coimbra with a pilgrim's staff, and King Manuel I, who made the pilgrimage from Lisbon to Santiago in 1502 and, the Xunta says, ordered that a lamp should be kept lit in the church at Santiago night and day. A queen and a king, and one lamp. You can walk for greater or lesser reasons than theirs. The road does not ask.
Questions for the walk
Take one a day, and do not hurry to answer.

items.t: What did you hope the first week would give you, and what is it giving you instead?
At what hour of the day do you feel most yourself: the early light, the long afternoon, the evening?
What are you carrying that you could leave behind, in your pack and elsewhere?
Who is walking with you in your head? Is there something you would like to say to them?
If the road asks nothing of you but the next step, what is your next step?
What would you like to bring home that you did not bring?

spans.t: If you walk for a faith, the road is also a place to pray, in your own way and at your own pace. If you walk for no faith at all, nothing here asks you to pretend. A road that has taken queens and kings, and tired people from every country, has room for you.
The last streets

On the last day the road crosses the valley of the Sar and the sanctuary of A Escravitude, and reaches O Milladoiro, where, the Xunta says, pilgrims knelt when they first saw the cathedral. The Xunta then describes the way into the old quarter by the Porta Faxeira and the Rúa do Franco, and says the traditional entrance for pilgrims on the Portuguese Way is through the square of As Praterías. The last stage, from Padrón, is ~25 km on the Xunta's figures.

Wikipedia says the cathedral was begun in 1075, a Romanesque building with later Gothic and Baroque additions. The Baroque façade on the Praza do Obradoiro was completed by Fernando de Casas Novoa in 1740, and the Pórtico da Gloria, the carved doorway behind it, by Master Mateo, in 1188.

The Holy Door is opened only in a Jacobean Holy Year, a year in which 25 July, the feast of St James, falls on a Sunday. Wikipedia lists the next as 2027 and 2032. The botafumeiro, the great censer, is swung on certain religious holidays, and at every Pilgrims' Mass in a Holy Year. If you walk this road in 2027, you may arrive in one.
Take a moment in the square before you do anything else. Sit on the stones if you like. After 27 days, the arrival may be quieter or noisier than you expected. There is no right feeling.
The Pilgrim's Office and the Compostela

The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago issues the Compostela. The rule it follows is in the chapter on other ways to split the days, and it is the Office's to apply. Bring your credencial, stamped along the way. To collect the Compostela you take a ticket with a QR code, which lets you follow your place in the queue, and the Office warns that in times of great influx it cannot guarantee same-day collection. Its website gives its address and its current hours, which are not in this book because they change.

If you walked for other reasons, or are unsure that yours count, the Office also offers a Certificate of Distance. It certifies the kilometres you travelled, whatever your starting point, and records the day and place you started, the day you arrived and the route. The Office says its reception service and the Compostela itself are free, and gives the price of the certificate, which is not in this book.
The Office meets a great many people in a day. Be patient, be warm, and if you have a doubt about your credencial, ask before you queue.
The pilgrims' Mass

The cathedral holds a Pilgrims' Mass. Look at the cathedral's own website for the time, which changes. You do not need to be a believer to sit at the back and listen. It is a cathedral full of people who have walked.
The next day
Try not to leave on the morning after you arrive. A day in Santiago lets the walk settle. Wash your clothes, sleep late, and look at the old town.
If you still have legs and time, some pilgrims walk on to Finisterre and Muxía, ~90 km farther, a route on the CaminoPlus app's list of routes that has its own book in this series,
To the End of the Earth
. If you do not, think about the way home: the next chapter helps.

You may come home with sore feet and an odd new sense of scale. After 27 days a four-hour bus journey may feel short, a kilometre may feel like nothing, and an ordinary week may feel too full. That is normal, and it passes slowly.
Getting home

Plan the return before you set out, with the timetables in front of you, not on the last day. The Confraternity notes a regular bus between Santiago and Porto in about four hours, so a flight home from either city is possible. Lisbon, where you began, has its own airport, ~7 km north-east of the historic centre, according to Wikipedia. How to get from Santiago back to Lisbon is not something this book can tell you: ask the app, the station and the airport, and check the current times.
Keeping the Way alive

Keep the credencial: it is now a record of a road. Write down what you remember in the first week at home, while it is still sharp: the plain in the early light, a town you reached tired, a word from someone you met. Keep walking, even for an hour a week, in the shoes you wore.
Walking again
You may find that you want another road. The Camino to Finisterre and Muxía, ~90 km from Santiago, has its own book in this series,
To the End of the Earth
. If you walked the Central road from Porto,
The Coastal Way
describes the sea road from Porto to the same cathedral. A road you have not walked is a good reason to come back.
Bom caminho
, again.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus

. The app is still in development. The route from Lisbon is on its list of routes, but its catalog holds no stages for it yet, so this book makes no claim about what the app holds for it today. Look in the app, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.

A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office asks for the stamped credencial. A passport in CaminoPlus, or in any app other than the Office's own digital credential, is a keepsake until the Office says otherwise.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and its fact ledger lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: , on its official Camino de Santiago portal: the page on the Portuguese Way, for its history, its two Portuguese pilgrims and the places of the road in Portugal, and the page on the last stage into Santiago.

, the regional tourism board: its guide to the Caminhos de Santiago in Central Portugal (2023), its sub-regional guide to the Médio Tejo (2024) and its English article on the Central Portuguese St James Way, for the towns of the road from Tomar to Grijó, the certification of the road in July 2023, and its advice to walkers.
, the Portuguese pilgrims' association: its pages on its aims, the credencial, the hostels and the Compostela.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
: the pages on the Compostela, the credencial and the Certificate of Distance.

: its page on the Camino Portugués, and a practical guide to the Lisbon to Porto stretch that presents itself as the Confraternity's own (a revised draft of December 2013, quoted in this book as the older sheet, and dated: its details may have changed).
for the road from Lisbon, from walking-holiday companies, named in the fact ledger. With the older sheet they give the stage towns and lengths, and they disagree, which is why the book says so.

, for climate tables, history and statistics: the articles on the Camino Portugués, Lisbon, Lisbon Cathedral, Lisbon Airport, the Parque das Nações, the Tagus, Vila Franca de Xira, Azambuja, Santarém, Golegã, Tomar, the Convent of Christ, Conímbriga, Coimbra, Alvaiázere, Albergaria-a-Velha, Oliveira de Azeméis, the Dom Luís I Bridge, Porto, Santiago de Compostela and its cathedral, the Jacobean Holy Year, and the time zones of Portugal and Spain.
and the app's own route note, for the route's start, end, ~620 km and difficulty rating.

spans.t: Visit Portugal's page on the road could not be read, because the site asks every visitor to pass a bot check, and nothing in this book rests on it. Published figures differ between these sources, so every distance is marked ~. Where the sources say nothing, the book says nothing, and tells you to check. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.

Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: Via Lusitana and the associations of friends of the Camino, who paint the arrows and keep the lists, the hosts who open their doors, and the people in the villages and towns who point the way and say
bom caminho
to a stranger.
A short glossary

: an old Portuguese word for a hostel for travellers.
: the wine country around Mealhada, known for sparkling wines and roast suckling pig.
: "good way", the Portuguese greeting between pilgrims; Spanish

: the Latin certificate the Pilgrim's Office issues.
